note: The idea behind all of Purgatory, set out in Canto 17: every sin is love aimed at the wrong thing, or in the wrong measure. Dante's Italian says this bad love leaves the gate unused: so few come through that it has grown stiff.
The angel's warning at the end of Canto 9: whoever looks back is put outside again.

quote: rolled and shifted side to side
note: Usually read as a narrow cleft that zigzags, so the climbers must keep to whichever wall bends away from them. Some take it that the rock itself moves.
The moon was full four nights ago, so it now sets well into the morning. The climb through the cleft has been slow.
Christ's saying in the Gospels: it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God. The way in is narrow.
The first of the seven terraces cut into the mountain, each cleansing one deadly sin. The lowest is for pride, the root of all the others and the heaviest to carry.
About five meters, or some eighteen feet, from the sheer drop to the cliff.

Every terrace begins by showing examples of the virtue opposed to its sin, and the first is always from the life of Mary. Here they are carvings of humility, set upright in the wall where souls bent double can still see them.
Dante names one: Polyclitus, the Greek sculptor of the fifth century BC, famous in the Middle Ages as the greatest of all.

context: The first carving is the Annunciation, from Luke's Gospel. The peace he announces is peace between God and humankind, longed for since Adam's fall shut Heaven.

note: In Latin, Ave: the angel's first word to Mary, and the opening of the prayer Hail Mary.

quote: the one who turned the key
context: By saying yes she opened the way for God's love to come into the world. She is the first example of humility: chosen above all women, she calls herself a servant.

quote: Behold the handmaid of the Lord
note: Mary's answer to the angel in Luke's Gospel, when she accepts what God asks of her.
The left side.

The Ark of the Covenant, the gilded chest that held the tablets of the Law, the holiest thing Israel owned. The second carving shows King David bringing it into Jerusalem, a story from the Second Book of Samuel.
On the way, the oxen stumbled and a man named Uzzah put out his hand to steady the ark. He was not a priest, and God struck him dead.
The carving is so lifelike that Dante's eyes tell him the choirs are singing, while his ears hear nothing. The same happens with the incense: his eyes see smoke, his nose smells none.

context: He danced before the ark with his robe hitched up like a servant. That made him less than a king in dignity, and more than a king in the eyes of God.

note: David's wife, the daughter of King Saul. She despised him for making a show of himself before the people, and the Bible says she remained childless. She is pride looking down on humility, from a palace window.
The third example comes from pagan history. Purgatory's lessons draw on the Bible and the ancient world side by side.

context: His "great victory" was over death and Hell. Legend said that Gregory, moved by the story of Trajan's justice, prayed for the pagan emperor's soul, and that God answered. Dante places Trajan in Heaven (Paradiso 20).
The story of the widow was a favorite of the Middle Ages. The master of the world, riding out to war with his army, stops for one poor woman and gives way to her argument.

note: The standards of the Roman legions. Dante pictures them as eagles on banners, like the flags of his own day, fluttering in the wind.

quote: He who never looked upon new things
note: God. Nothing can be new to him, since he sees all things at once and forever.
A famous phrase: visibile parlare. The whole exchange between Trajan and the widow is read off the stone, as if a carving could hold a conversation. No human art can do it.
Dante breaks in before showing the punishment, afraid the sight will discourage the reader from repenting. The pain is real, but it is a debt being paid off, and it ends.
Purgatory is temporary. At the Last Judgment, at the end of time, it will be emptied, and every soul in it will be in Heaven.
The punishment answers the sin. Those who carried their heads high in life are bent double under boulders, their faces forced toward the ground. The heavier the pride, the heavier the stone.
Dante turns on the living. Pride is the sin he admits most readily in himself: in Canto 13 he says he already feels the weight of these stones.
The soul. Human beings on earth are caterpillars, and what matters is the winged thing that comes out at death and goes to be judged. The butterfly was an ancient image of the soul.
A bracket that holds up a beam or a roof. Medieval builders often carved them as crouching human figures, knees to chest, who seem to be crushed by the weight.
Even the most patient of them is at the limit of his strength. The canto stops here, before any of the proud has been named.
